Chapter 1: Foundations of Strategy — Seeing the World as a Field of Practice
Every journey toward mastery really starts with knowing exactly where you stand. In strategy, that means realizing every action—whether it’s on the battlefield, in the boardroom, or just in your daily routine—follows the same core principles. Instead of seeing life as a bunch of separate events, try looking at it as one continuous field. Skills, intentions, and outcomes are always shifting and interacting.
Here’s the thing—strategy isn’t just for warriors or business leaders. It’s a way of seeing and responding to any kind of challenge or competition you face. Whether you’re up against a rival, working through a negotiation, or just navigating something tricky in your personal life, those same strategic habits apply. And when you start treating every situation as a chance to practice and refine how you respond, you’ll be amazed at how much you grow.
One of the biggest foundations of strategy is disciplined practice. Mastery doesn’t come from talent alone—it’s built through repeating the basics with real focus. Think about a skilled carpenter. They don’t just know their tools—they use them with care and precision, over and over, until it’s second nature. If you want to get better at anything—whether it’s using a sword, speaking up in meetings, or sharing new ideas—you’ve got to get intimately familiar with your own set of tools. That means going back to the fundamentals, again and again, until they truly stick with you.
Let’s talk about a few core habits that help you build a strong foundation in strategy:
First, treat every encounter as a real opportunity to learn and improve.
Second, keep your focus on the basics—practice them until they’re deeply ingrained.
And third, always try to observe what’s happening with a clear, unbiased mind, free from any old assumptions.
This whole approach is grounded in realism. Instead of chasing perfect ideals or sticking to rigid rules, the best strategists are honest about what actually works. That means being upfront about your own strengths and weaknesses, and noticing those in others, too. No single method is perfect every time, so it’s way more important to be flexible and adaptable than to cling to tradition.
Picture a craftsman who doesn’t just use one tool for every job—they choose the right one for each task. In the same way, a good strategist adapts their methods to fit the moment. That takes a willingness to experiment, to make mistakes, and to shift your approach if things aren’t working out.
So, the real foundation of strategy isn’t just a set of techniques—it’s a whole way of seeing and engaging with the world. It’s about committing to continuous learning, rooted in what actually happens, and keeping an open mind. With this mindset, you’re laying the groundwork for deeper insights and lasting success.
